In theory, one flick of your finger could knock down the Eiffel Tower.
All you'd need is twenty-eight dominoes.
A falling domino can topple another one about one and a half times its size.
So start with a tiny one. Just five millimetres tall.
By the thirteenth, it's sixty-five centimetres, and it hits with nearly three hundred million times the energy of your flick.
The twenty-fourth is taller than the Arc de Triomphe.
The twenty-seventh is almost as tall as the Montparnasse Tower.
And the twenty-eighth, two hundred and eighty-four metres tall, brings down the Eiffel Tower.
Each step is only one and a half times bigger. But it carries about five times the energy. Compounding does the rest.
Small things, passed along, don't stay small. A mistake. A rumour. A bad morning.
The fix is a gap. A space the next one can't reach.
In life, that gap is slack. Money in the bank. Room in your calendar. A pause before you reply.
Leave a gap, and one fall stays one fall.
